title: Saving Time, Shortening Journeys
subtitle: How India’s Infrastructure Is Bringing Places Closer
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                05 OCT 2026 12:37PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Connectivity Measured in Hours Saved
For millions of travellers, better connectivity is measured in hours saved, not only in kilometres built. Across India, new bridges, tunnels, expressways and rail services are changing the time it takes to travel between cities, regions and communities. By replacing detours, difficult terrain and slow routes with direct and faster connections, these projects are making infrastructure-led transformation visible in everyday travel. As faster links reach more parts of the country, distance is becoming less of a constraint on everyday mobility.
Bridges: Crossing Barriers, Cutting Travel Time
Bridges are removing long and slow river crossings from everyday travel and turning journeys that once took hours into much shorter trips.
Bhupen Hazarika Setu/ Dhola–Sadiya Bridge, Assam–Arunachal Pradesh ( May, 2017)
6 hours → 1 hour
Travel time between Rupai in Assam and Meka/Roing in Arunachal Pradesh has fallen from six hours to one hour, saving
five hours
.
Bogibeel Bridge, Assam (December, 2018)
A day-long journey → 1–2 hours
The rail-cum-road bridge over the Brahmaputra has transformed connectivity between Dhemaji and Dibrugarh. Journeys that earlier took almost an entire day now take about one to two hours.
Atal Setu, Maharashtra (January, 2024)
2 hours → 20 minutes
The Mumbai Trans Harbour Link provides a direct connection between Mumbai and Navi Mumbai, cutting the journey to about 20 minutes.
Kosi Rail Mahasetu, Bihar (September, 2020)
8 hours → 30 minutes
The Kosi Rail Mahasetu reduced the rail journey between Nirmali and Saraigarh from about eight hours to 30 minutes, while reducing the distance from about 300 km to 22 km.
Sisseri River Bridge, Arunachal Pradesh (November, 2019)
About 5 hours saved
The 200-metre Sisseri River Bridge reduced the travel time between
Pasighat and Roing by about five hours
, strengthening connectivity between Dibang Valley and Siang.
Tunnels: Cutting Through Terrain, Saving Hours
Tunnels are taking the shortest route through some of India’s most difficult terrain. Bypassing mountains, winding roads and vulnerable stretches, they are bringing down travel times while making journeys seamless.
Atal Tunnel, Himachal Pradesh (October, 2020)
4–5 hours saved
The 9.02-km tunnel bypasses Rohtang Pass and reduces the Manali–Sarchu distance by
46 km
, providing all-weather connectivity to Lahaul-Spiti.
Dr. Syama Prasad Mookerjee Tunnel, Jammu & Kashmir (April, 2017)
Nearly 2 hours saved
The 9-km tunnel bypasses difficult terrain, cuts the travel distance by about
30 km
and reduces travel time between Jammu and Srinagar by nearly two hours.
Banihal–Qazigund Road Tunnel, Jammu & Kashmir (April, 2022)
~1.5 hours saved
The 8.45-km twin-tube tunnel cuts the road distance by
16 km
and reduces journey time by around one and a half hours.
Sela Tunnel, Arunachal Pradesh (March, 2024)
Travel time cut by over 1 hour
Built at an altitude of about 13,000 feet, the tunnel ensures all-weather connectivity on the strategically important Tezpur-Tawang route.
Expressways & Economic Corridors
Expressways are changing the pace of inter-city travel through shorter alignments, controlled access and higher speeds. Long journeys that once consumed several hours are being compressed into significantly faster road trips.
Delhi–Meerut Expressway (2021)
2.5 hours → 50 minutes
The 82-km project reduced travel time between Delhi and Meerut from around two and a half hours to about 50 minutes.
Bengaluru–Mysuru Expressway (March, 2023)
3 hours → 75 minutes
The 118-km expressway has reduced travel time between Bengaluru and Mysuru from nearly three hours to about 75 minutes.
Delhi–Dehradun Economic Corridor (April, 2026)
6 hours → 2.5 hours
The 213-km access-controlled corridor reduces travel time between Delhi and Dehradun from over six hours to around two and a half hours.
Mumbai–Nagpur Samruddhi Mahamarg (December, 2022)
16 hours → ~8 hours
The 701-km access-controlled expressway has substantially reduced travel time between Mumbai and Nagpur.
Ahmedabad–Dholera Expressway (March, 2026)
Ahmedabad- Dholera: from 100 km & 2 hr 15 min → 83 km & 45 min
Ahmedabad to Bhavnagar: from 169 km & 3 hr 15 min → 141 km & 1 hr 45 min
The access-controlled greenfield expressway stretching over 109 km provides a high-speed link between Ahmedabad and Dholera.
Delhi–Amritsar–Katra Expressway (Phase-I- July, 2026)
Delhi–Amritsar: 8 hours → 4 hours
Delhi–Katra: 14 hours → 6 hours
The expressway is being developed to boost pilgrim and tourist traffic to Shri Mata Vaishno Devi, and catalyse industrial and logistics development along the corridor.
Delhi–Mumbai Expressway
33 hours → ~12 hours
The greenfield expressway is being developed to reduce travel time between Delhi and Mumbai to about 12 hours from roughly 33 hours.
Railways: Faster Trains, Shorter Journeys
New-generation trains and dedicated high-speed corridors are bringing major time savings to rail travel. The 2026 railway timetable reflects this shift, with 549 trains speeded up across the network. Of these, 20 trains became faster by 60 minutes or more. Another 48 trains gained 31–59 minutes, while 105 trains gained 16–30 minutes. The remaining 376 trains were speeded up by 5–15 minutes.
New Generation Trains
Vande Bharat Express, New Delhi–Varanasi (February, 2019)
40–50% faster than earlier services
India's first Vande Bharat was launched on
15 February 2019
on the New Delhi–Kanpur–Prayagraj–Varanasi corridor. The scheduled travel time between New Delhi and Varanasi is approximately eight hours, making it around 40-50% faster than earlier services on the route.
Vande Bharat Express, Katra–Srinagar (June, 2025)
2–3 hours saved
The train cut Katra–Srinagar travel to
about three hours
. The extended Jammu–Srinagar service now covers the journey in
4 hours 50 minutes
.
Vande Bharat Express, Banaras–Khajuraho (November, 2025)
~2 hours 40 minutes saved
The train saves about 2 hours 40 minutes compared with the special trains earlier in operation.
Vande Bharat Express, Ernakulam–Bengaluru (November, 2025)
Over 2 hours saved
The service covers the journey in
8 hours 40 minutes
, reducing travel time by over two hours.
Vande Bharat Express, Lucknow–Saharanpur (November, 2025)
Nearly 1 hour saved
The train completes the journey in approximately
7 hours 45 minutes
.
Vande Bharat Sleeper, Howrah–Guwahati (January, 2026)
~17 hours → ~14 hours
India's first Vande Bharat Sleeper saves
nearly three hours
over the Saraighat Express. It has 16 air-conditioned coaches for around 823 passengers.
High-Speed Rail Corridors
Mumbai–Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail Corridor
8–9 hours by road → ~1 hour 58 minutes
The
508-km
corridor, with an operational speed of 320 kmph, will serve 12 stations. It includes India's first undersea rail tunnel, about 7 km beneath Thane Creek. The first service is targeted for
August 2027
.
Seven Announced High-Speed Rail (HSR) Corridors
Major city pairs within about 1–4 hours
Announced in the Union Budget 2026–27, the corridors span
nearly 4,000 km
with an estimated investment of
₹16 lakh crore
.
Corridor
Indicative travel time
Delhi–Varanasi
~3 hours 50 minutes
Varanasi–Patna–Siliguri
~2 hours 55 minutes
Chennai–Bengaluru
~1 hour 13 minutes
Bengaluru–Hyderabad
~2 hours
Chennai–Hyderabad
~2 hours 55 minutes
Mumbai–Pune
~48 minutes
Pune–Hyderabad
~1 hour 55 minutes
Hours Returned to Travellers and Communities
The transformation of India’s transport network is changing how people and regions connect with one another. Bridges and tunnels are opening new crossings while expressways and modern rail services are redefining long-distance travel. Together, these interventions are making mobility more seamless and expanding access across regions.

Interaction with representatives of civil society, NGOs and Human Rights Defenders also scheduled
date:

content:
The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), India is holding a two-day ‘Open Hearing and Camp Sitting’ at Gyan Bhawan, Patna, Bihar on 7th - 8th October 2026 to hear cases of alleged human rights violations in the State.
On Day-1, NHRC Chairperson, Justice V. Ramasubramanian and Members, Justice (Dr.) Bidyut Ranjan Sarangi and Smt. Vijaya Bharathi Sayani will hear cases
in the
Full Commission sitting in the presence of complainants and concerned officers of the State.
The next day, on 8th October 2026, the Commission will hear cases in two separate Benches. The Chairperson will hear cases of alleged bonded labour. Simultaneously, a Division Bench, comprising Members, Justice (Dr.) Bidyut Ranjan Sarangi and Smt. Vijaya Bharathi Sayani, will hear cases related to compliance matters and other complaints of alleged violation of human rights.
Thereafter, the Commission will interact with representatives of civil society organisations, NGOs and Human Rights Defenders. In the concluding session, the Commission will hold a meeting of senior officers to discuss important human rights issues pertaining to the State.
The NHRC, India has been holding Camp Sittings from time to time in various States since 2007 to facilitate easy access to justice for the victims of human rights violations.

title: Union Minister of State for Chemicals and Fertilizers Anupriya Patel Launches 14th Edition of India Chem 2026
subtitle:
Chemicals and Petrochemicals Sector Can Become a Key Growth Engine of Indian Economy: Anupriya Patel

India Chem 2026 to be Held in Mumbai from October 22 to 24
ministry: Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers :Department of Chemicals and Petrochemicals
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                05 OCT 2026 10:13PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister of State for Chemicals and Fertilizers and Health and Family Welfare, Smt. Anupriya Patel, today launched the 14th edition of India Chem 2026, the biennial flagship event of the chemicals and petrochemicals industry. The event will be held in Mumbai from October 22 to 24, 2026.
Addressing the launch event in New Delhi, Smt. Anupriya Patel said that the Government is committed to creating a conducive ecosystem and strengthening infrastructure for the industry to make India self-reliant and realise the vision of a developed India by 2047.
The Minister said that the chemicals and petrochemicals sector has potential to emerge as an important growth engine of the Indian economy. She emphasised the need to align key national initiatives, including the Critical Mineral Mission, Rare Earth Corridor, India Semiconductor Mission 2.0, National Manufacturing Mission and FDI reforms, to position India as a global hub for battery chemicals, speciality chemicals and semiconductor chemicals by 2040.
Speaking on the BHAVYA Rasayan Scheme, the Minister said that the scheme should not be viewed as just an infrastructure program but as an attempt to create an environment in which the chemicals and petrochemicals industry can innovate, invest and expand. It was mentioned that the guidelines of the scheme have been released and urged the industry to engage with the state governments for timely submission of the proposals.
The Minister urged industry to increase the spending on R&D along with adopting newer technologies. She further stated that the Department is already pursuing the Department of Science and Technology to declare chemicals and petrochemicals as a priority sector so that it will be covered under the new Research Development Innovation Scheme (RDI) which has an outlay of about 1 lakh Crores. She added that these initiatives would contribute towards achieving the vision of developing the Indian chemical sector into a USD 1 trillion industry by 2040.
Addressing the gathering, Secretary, Department of Chemicals and Petrochemicals (DCPC), Shri Tejveer Singh, said that the chemicals sector forms the bedrock of India's economic growth and development.
Highlighting the initiatives of the Department, the DCPC Secretary mentioned that the vision of dedicated chemical parks is now close to seeing reality in form of BHAVYA Rasayan scheme. These parks will have best in class facilities including plug and play, proper infrastructure and other facilities so that we are able to bring efficiencies in the cost of production. He also emphasised the need to increase investment in research and development (R&D), stating that sustained investment in R&D is imperative for the growth, innovation and global competitiveness of the sector. He further stated that the Department is working with DPIIT on import substitution exercises in which the chemical and petrochemical sector is included.
Shri Deepankar Aron, Joint Secretary, Department of Chemicals & Petrochemicals, Govt. of India while making a presentation on India Chem, mentioned that the aim of the event, which is now in its 14th edition, is to attract investments in the sector along with facilitating B2B partnerships enabling the sector to work together towards growth.
Shri Prabh Das, Chairman, FICCI National Petrochemicals & Plastics Committee and MD & CEO, HPCL-Mittal Energy Ltd., stated that India needs to focus on increased production and there is full support from the Government for the same.
Shri S Ganeshkumar, Co-Chair, FICCI Chemicals Committee and MD, Chemplast Sanmar Ltd said that India’s chemical sector is fully capable to absorb massive capital, leverage FDIs and position itself as the world’s most lucrative chemical industry.
India Chem 2026 is being hosted by the Department of Chemicals and Petrochemicals in partnership with the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI). The 14th edition of the biennial event will comprise an international exhibition and conference, bringing together key stakeholders from the chemicals and petrochemicals sector, including industry leaders, policymakers, investors, researchers and international participants. The event will have sector specific Conclaves on Agrochemicals, Petrochemicals, Speciality Chemicals, as well as on Infrastructure, Environment issues and Process, plant and Machinery. Apart from above, region specific Forums of India-US, India-EU, India-Russia, India-Japan will also take place.
The theme of India Chem 2026 is “Advantage Bharat: An Emerging Global Hub”, reflecting India's growing capabilities and expanding opportunities in the global chemicals and petrochemicals sector.
